mainTopic: יאוש שלא מדעת: the argument between אביי and רבא, and the proofs tested against it
overview: The גמרא presents a famous argument between אביי and רבא about יאוש שלא מדעת. This is the case where the owner would surely give up on his lost item, but he does not yet know it is lost. אביי says this does not count as יאוש, and רבא says it does. The גמרא narrows the argument. If the item has a סימן, everyone agrees there is no יאוש. The one exception is items swept away by the sea or a flooding river, which the Torah lets the finder keep. The real argument is only about items with no סימן. The גמרא then brings a long list of proofs for רבא: scattered produce, coins, fig cakes and loaves, purple wool, coins in crowded places, and לקט. Each one is rejected by showing the owner really did know about his loss. A משנה about fallen figs, olives and carobs is then shown to fit both sides, with the help of רבי אבהו and רב פפא. Finally, the גמרא begins a new proof from a ברייתא about a גנב or גזלן who passed an item to someone else, and that proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: אביי and רבא argue about despair the owner does not know about
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules that יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש, and רבא rules that it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Despair that happens without the owner knowing: אביי said it is not despair, and רבא said it is despair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a famous argument. Does an owner give up on his item (יאוש) if he does not yet know it is lost, even though he would give up once he found out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a finder may keep a lost item once the owner has despaired of getting it back. Here the owner has not actually despaired yet, because he does not know about the loss. אביי says only real, conscious despair counts. רבא says the despair that is sure to come is already enough.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner's giving up hope of getting his lost item back
Without awareness; the owner does not yet know about the loss

steps.whyThisMatters: This is one of the six famous cases where the הלכה follows אביי against רבא (יע"ל קג"ם). It shapes the laws of lost objects throughout this perek.

phrases.english: Despair that is not with awareness:
phrases.notes: He means the owner would surely give up if he knew, but right now he has no idea the item is lost.

phrases.english: Abaye said: It is not despair.
And Rava said: It is despair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the sugya
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש. רבא: it is יאוש.

steps.title: With an identifying mark, everyone agrees it is not despair
steps.stepSummary: If the item has a סימן, both sides agree it is not יאוש, even if the owner later gives up, because the finder picked it up when taking it was still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: With an item that has an identifying mark, everyone agrees it is not despair. Even if we later hear that the owner gave up, it still does not count. When the item came into the finder's hands, it came in a forbidden way. When the owner first learns it fell, he does not despair. He says: 'I have a mark on it. I will give the mark and take it back.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts narrowing the argument. When the item has a סימן, both אביי and רבא agree it is not יאוש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner whose item has a סימן does not give up when he first finds out. He expects to identify it and get it back. So when the finder picked it up, the item still fully belonged to the owner, and taking it was forbidden. Despair that comes later cannot make a forbidden pickup into a permitted one.

keyTerms.meaning: An identifying mark that lets the owner prove the item is his
Everyone agrees; there is no argument here

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the owner's later despair helps the finder. What matters is the moment the finder picked the item up. At that moment, taking it was forbidden.

phrases.english: With an item that has an identifying mark,
everyone agrees
that it is not despair.
And even though we hear him
that he despairs in the end, it is not despair,
because when it came into his hand,
phrases.notes: 'His hand' here means the finder's hand.

phrases.english: it was in a forbidden way that it came into his hand,
for when he learns that it fell from him,
he does not despair; rather, he says:
'I have an identifying mark on it;
I will give the mark and take it back.'

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּדָבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ סִימָן כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the scope of the argument in step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An item with a סימן is not under יאוש שלא מדעת for anyone, because the finder's pickup happened while taking it was forbidden.

steps.title: Items swept away by sea or river are an exception
steps.stepSummary: Items carried off by the sea's tide or a river's flood may be kept by the finder even if they have a סימן, because the Torah allows it.
steps.simpleTranslation: With the tide of the sea or the flooding of a river, even though the item has a mark, the Torah permits the finder to keep it, as we will explain later.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a side note: there is one exception to the rule about items with a סימן. Items swept away by the sea or a flooding river may be kept even if they have a mark.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exception does not come from the logic of יאוש. It is a special permission from the Torah (רחמנא שרייה). The גמרא promises to explain where it comes from later in the sugya.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah (literally 'the Merciful One') permits it
Later on; further along in the discussion

phrases.english: With the tide of the sea
and with the flooding of a river,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִית בֵּיהּ סִימָן,
phrases.english: even though it has an identifying mark,
the Torah permits it,
as we will say later on.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּזוּטוֹ שֶׁל יָם וּבִשְׁלוּלִיתוֹ שֶׁל נָהָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception to the rule in step 2
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Items lost to the sea or a river flood may be kept even with a סימן, by the Torah's permission.

steps.title: The real argument: items with no identifying mark
steps.stepSummary: The argument is only about items without a סימן. אביי says there is no יאוש because the owner doesn't know of the loss. רבא says there is, because the owner will surely despair, so his despair counts from now.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about an item with no identifying mark. אביי said it is not despair, because the owner doesn't know it fell from him. רבא said it is despair, because when he learns it fell he will despair. He will say, 'I have no mark on it,' so he counts as despairing from now.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states exactly where אביי and רבא disagree: an item with no סימן. It gives each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי looks at the owner's actual state of mind. He hasn't given up, because he doesn't know anything happened. רבא looks at what is sure to happen. With no סימן, the owner will surely give up once he finds out, so we treat his despair as already in place from the moment the item fell. The question is whether certain future despair counts right now.
steps.whatToRemember: With a סימן, everyone agrees there is no יאוש (except items lost to sea or river). Without a סימן: אביי says unknown despair doesn't count, and רבא says it counts from the moment of loss.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן.
phrases.english: Where they disagree is with an item that has no identifying mark.
Abaye said: It is not despair,
because he does not know that it fell from him.
Rava said: It is despair,
because when he learns that it fell from him, he will despair.

phrases.aramaic: מֵימָר אָמַר: סִימָנָא לֵית לִי בְּגַוֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: He says: 'I have no identifying mark on it,'
so it is from now that he despairs.
phrases.notes: 'From now' means from the moment the item fell, even before the owner noticed.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After setting aside items with a סימן, pinpoints where the argument from step 1 applies
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For an item without a סימן: אביי says no יאוש because the owner is unaware. רבא says יאוש counts from the moment of loss, since the despair is certain.

steps.title: A memory aid for the coming list of proofs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a string of letters to help remember the order of the proofs that come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: (Memory aid: פמג״ש ממקגט״י ככסע״ז)
steps.whatsHappening: Before bringing a long list of proofs about אביי and רבא, the גמרא gives a memory aid. This line sets up the series of proofs that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each letter hints at one of the cases the גמרא will bring. It adds no new law. It only helps the learner keep the long list in order.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: a memory aid made of letters, one for each case that follows

steps.confusionAlert: In Step 2, סימן meant an identifying mark on a lost item. Here סימן means something different: a memory aid for the list of proofs.

phrases.english: (Memory aid: P-M-G-Sh, M-M-K-G-T-Y, K-K-S-A-Z)
phrases.notes: Each letter stands for one case coming up, like פ for פירות and מ for מעות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the list of proofs that will test the argument laid out in Step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling; this is only a memory aid for the coming proofs.

steps.title: Proof from scattered produce
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says a finder keeps scattered produce, even though the owner may not know it fell. This seems to support רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: scattered produce belongs to the finder. But the owner does not know it fell from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the משנה's case of scattered produce, which the finder may keep. It suggests this proves רבא, since the owner doesn't even know he lost it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the finder keeps the produce, the owner must have given up on it. The owner did not know about the loss, so this would be יאוש שלא מדעת. That would show רבא is right and challenge אביי.

keyTerms.meaning: Giving up on an item without knowing it was lost

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Scattered produce [belongs to the finder],
But he does not know that it fell from him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First proof from the list introduced by the memory aid. It tests the argument from Step 4.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת counts as יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: scattered produce belongs to the finder

steps.title: The produce was left behind on purpose
steps.stepSummary: רב עוקבא בר חמא explained that the משנה means kernels left at the threshing floor, which the owner left knowingly. So the owner knew, and there is no proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't רב עוקבא בר חמא say: here we are dealing with grain gathered at the threshing floor, which is a loss the owner knows about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the proof aside by using רב עוקבא בר חמא's explanation of the case. The produce was left on purpose at the threshing floor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner knowingly left the leftover kernels behind, so he gave up on them with full knowledge. That is not יאוש שלא מדעת at all. So this case says nothing about the argument between אביי and רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: A loss the owner knows about, here something left behind on purpose

phrases.aramaic: הָא אָמַר רַב עוּקְבָא בַּר חָמָא:
phrases.english: But didn't Rav Ukva bar Chama say:
Here, with the gathering
at the threshing floors, we are dealing,
phrases.notes: Some versions have דביזרי, in round brackets; the corrected wording, in square brackets, is דבי דרי, threshing floors.

phrases.english: which is a loss the owner knows about.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא אָמַר רַב עוּקְבָא בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 6 by redefining the case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof from scattered produce
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the owner didn't know. In fact he left the kernels on purpose, so his giving up was knowing.

steps.title: Proof from scattered coins
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says scattered coins belong to the finder, even though the owner may not know they fell. This seems to support רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: scattered coins belong to the finder. Why? The owner doesn't know they fell from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second proof from the משנה: scattered coins. Coins usually fall without the owner noticing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Coins have no identifying mark, and the finder keeps them. If the owner did not know he lost them, his giving up would be יאוש שלא מדעת, which supports רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: These belong to him, the finder

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Scattered coins:
these belong to him.

phrases.aramaic: אַמַּאי? הָא לָא יָדַע דִּנְפַל מִינֵּיהּ!
phrases.english: Why? He does not know that they fell from him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof fell, the גמרא tries a second case from the same משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת counts as יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: scattered coins belong to the finder

steps.title: People check their pockets all the time
steps.stepSummary: Following רבי יצחק, a person feels his money pouch constantly, so he soon notices the coins are gone. His giving up is knowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, it follows רבי יצחק, who said: a person regularly feels his pouch at every moment. Here too, a person regularly feels his pouch at every moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the coin proof. It uses רבי יצחק's rule that people constantly check their money pouch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because people keep touching their pouch, the owner finds out about the loss almost right away and gives up knowingly. So this is not יאוש שלא מדעת, and nothing is proven for רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: To feel or check his money pouch

phrases.english: There too, it is like Rabbi Yitzchak, who said:
A person tends to feel his pouch
at every moment.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי אָדָם עָשׂוּי לְמַשְׁמֵשׁ בְּכִיסוֹ
phrases.english: Here too, a person tends to feel his pouch
at every moment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof from scattered coins
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the owner didn't know. In fact people check their pouch constantly, so he quickly knows and gives up knowingly.

steps.title: Proof from fig cakes and baker's loaves
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says round fig cakes and baker's loaves belong to the finder, even though the owner may not know they fell. This seems to support רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: round cakes of pressed figs and baker's loaves belong to the finder. Why? Doesn't the owner not know they fell from him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a third case from the משנה: fig cakes and bakery loaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These items are kept by the finder. Once again the owner seemingly didn't notice the loss, so this looks like יאוש שלא מדעת working, as רבא holds.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Round cakes of pressed figs
and a baker's loaves:
these belong to him.

phrases.aramaic: אַמַּאי? וְהָא לָא יָדַע דִּנְפַל מִינֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: Why? Doesn't he not know that they fell from him?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: עִיגּוּלֵי דְבֵילָה וְכִכָּרוֹת שֶׁל נַחְתּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the coin proof fell, the גמרא tries a third case from the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת counts as יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: fig cakes and baker's loaves belong to the finder

steps.title: Heavy items are missed right away
steps.stepSummary: Fig cakes and loaves are heavy, so the owner notices right away when they fall. His giving up is knowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, since they are heavy, he surely knows about them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the third proof. Heavy items are noticed as soon as they fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The weight of these items makes the loss obvious to the owner. So he knew and gave up knowingly. Like the earlier cases, this is not יאוש שלא מדעת, and אביי's view is not disproven.
steps.whatToRemember: All three cases from the משנה (produce, coins, fig cakes and loaves) fail as proofs for רבא. In each one the owner really did know about the loss, so his giving up was knowing.

phrases.english: There too,
since they are heavy,
he surely knows about them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי, אַגַּב דְּיַקִּירֵי מִידָּע יָדַע בְּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof from fig cakes and loaves
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the owner didn't know. In fact heavy items are missed right away, so he gave up knowingly.

steps.title: Proof from strips of purple wool
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says strips of purple wool belong to the finder, even though the owner may not know they fell. This seems to support רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: strips of purple wool belong to the finder. But why? The owner doesn't know they fell from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another line of the משנה to try to prove that יאוש שלא מדעת counts as יאוש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finder keeps the wool, so the owner must have given up on it. But the owner may not even know it fell yet. If the finder can still keep it, that would show that not-yet-knowing יאוש still works, just as רבא says.

keyTerms.meaning: And why? Opens the question that drives the proof
Giving up without knowing: the owner would give up if he knew, but he doesn't know yet

phrases.english: Come and hear: and strips of purple wool
these belong to him.
And why?
He doesn't know that it fell from him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another proof from the same משנה, after the fig cakes proof was rejected in Step 11.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת is יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's ruling that strips of purple wool belong to the finder

steps.title: Valuable items are checked often
steps.stepSummary: Purple wool is valuable, so the owner keeps feeling for it and notices quickly when it is gone. His giving up is knowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, since they are valuable, he keeps feeling for them, like רבי יצחק's teaching.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the wool proof by saying the owner really did know about his loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the wool is expensive, the owner keeps checking that it is still there. So he finds out soon after it falls, and his יאוש is knowing. This is the same reasoning רבי יצחק used for coins in Step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: There too: the same answer as before applies here

phrases.english: There too,
since they are valuable,
he keeps feeling for them,
and this is like רבי יצחק's teaching.
phrases.notes: This points back to Step 9: a person feels his money pouch all the time.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי, אַגַּב דַּחֲשִׁיבִי מַשְׁמוּשֵׁי מְמַשְׁמֵשׁ בְּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only this proof for רבא is rejected. אביי's view is not disproven by it.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the owner didn't know. In fact, valuable items are checked often, so he soon knew.

steps.title: Proof from coins found in a busy place
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says coins found in a synagogue, a study hall or any crowded place belong to the finder because the owner gives up. But the owner may not know they fell.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one who finds coins in synagogues, study halls, or any place where many people are found keeps them, because the owners give up on them. But doesn't the owner not know they fell?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries another proof for רבא, this time from a ברייתא about coins in public places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא openly gives the reason: the owners give up. Since the owner may not know yet that the coins fell, this looks like יאוש שלא מדעת that still works.

keyTerms.meaning: A place where many people are found, a crowded public place
They give up hope of getting it back

phrases.english: Come and hear: one who finds coins
in synagogues and in study halls,
and in any place where many people are found,
these belong to him,
because the owners give up on them.
But doesn't he not know that it fell from him?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הַמּוֹצֵא מָעוֹת בְּבָתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new proof from a ברייתא, after the wool proof was rejected.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת is יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about coins found in synagogues and crowded places

steps.title: People check their pouch all the time
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק says a person feels his money pouch constantly, so he quickly knows his coins are gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: a person tends to feel his pouch all the time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the coin proof using רבי יצחק's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since people keep touching their money pouch, the owner discovers the loss almost right away. So his giving up is knowing, and this proof does not help רבא.

phrases.english: רבי יצחק said:
a person tends to feel his pouch
all the time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: אָדָם עָשׂוּי לְמַשְׁמֵשׁ בְּכִיסוֹ בְּכׇל שָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the coin proof is rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The owner does know, because he keeps checking his pouch.

steps.title: Proof from gleanings: when may anyone take them
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says that anyone, not just the poor, may take לקט once the נמושות have walked through the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: from when may everyone take לקט? Once the נמושות have walked through the field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source about לקט. Here it is only setting up the proof; the actual question comes in Step 18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לקט belongs only to the poor. The משנה says that after a certain point, anyone may take it, which means the poor have given up on it. The גמרא will soon ask how this works for poor people who are not there.

keyTerms.meaning: Gleanings: stalks that fall during harvest, which the Torah gives to the poor
A group of late gleaners; Step 17 explains exactly who they are

phrases.english: Come and hear: from when
is everyone permitted to take the gleanings?
phrases.notes: 'Everyone' means even people who are not poor.

phrases.english: Once the נמושות have walked through it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מֵאֵימָתַי כׇּל אָדָם מוּתָּרִים בַּלֶּקֶט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the coin proof was rejected, a new source is brought.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת is יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about when everyone may take לקט

steps.title: Who are the נמושות?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says they are old people who walk with a cane. ריש לקיש says they are a second round of gleaners.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we asked: what are נמושות? רבי יוחנן said: old people who walk with a cane. ריש לקיש said: gleaners after the gleaners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to explain a hard word in the משנה before it makes its point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both explanations describe the last people to go through the field carefully. Old people walk slowly and spot every stalk, and a second round of gleaners picks up what the first round missed. After them, the poor give up on what is left.

keyTerms.meaning: Gleaners after gleaners, a second round

phrases.english: And we asked: what are נמושות?
And רבי יוחנן said:
old people who walk on a cane.
ריש לקיש said:
gleaners after gleaners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains a word from the source quoted in Step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the word נמושות mean?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יוחנן: old people with canes. ריש לקיש: a second round of gleaners.

steps.title: What about poor people somewhere else?
steps.stepSummary: The poor who are here gave up, but poor people elsewhere don't know and haven't given up. Still, anyone may take the לקט, so this seems to support רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why? Fine, the poor here gave up, but there are poor people in another place who did not give up!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא makes the actual proof from the לקט משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לקט belongs to all poor people, including those in other towns. They do not know that the נמושות passed through, so any יאוש of theirs is not knowing. If anyone may still take the לקט, it looks like יאוש שלא מדעת works.

phrases.english: And why?
Granted that the poor here give up,
there are poor people in another place
who do not give up!
phrases.notes: They haven't given up because they don't know the field has already been gleaned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining the term, the גמרא returns to the proof begun in Step 16.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת is יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The לקט משנה: anyone may take it, even though poor people elsewhere don't know to give up

steps.title: Poor people far away gave up from the start
steps.stepSummary: Since there are poor people here, the poor elsewhere gave up from the very beginning. They figure the local poor will gather it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: since there are poor people here, those others gave up from the start, saying: the poor over there will gather it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the לקט proof. The faraway poor did give up, and they did it knowingly from the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The faraway poor never expected to get this field's לקט, because they know the local poor will take it. So their giving up happened from the very beginning, and it was knowing. This is not יאוש שלא מדעת at all.
steps.whatToRemember: Each proof for רבא in this section (wool, coins in public places, לקט) was rejected the same way: in every case the owner really did know and gave up knowingly.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the faraway poor 'don't count'. They do have a share; they simply gave up on it knowingly from the start.

phrases.english: They said:
since there are poor people here,
those others gave up from the start,
phrases.notes: 'Those others' are the poor in other places.

phrases.english: and they say: the poor over there will gather it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the לקט proof is rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The faraway poor are not unaware givers-up. They gave up knowingly from the beginning.

steps.title: A משנה about fallen figs, olives and carobs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה. Fallen dried figs and figs under a tree that leans over a road are permitted and exempt from מעשר. Fallen olives and carobs are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: dried figs found on the road, even next to a field of dried figs, and also figs found under a fig tree that leans over the road, may be taken. This is not stealing, and they are exempt from מעשר. But olives and carobs are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new משנה to test the dispute between אביי and רבא about יאוש שלא מדעת. This step sets up the source, and the next steps check how it fits each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these cases the owner almost certainly does not yet know that his fruit fell. So if taking the fruit is allowed, that suggests giving up without knowing still counts (רבא). If it is forbidden, that suggests it does not count (אביי). The משנה permits figs but forbids olives and carobs, so each side has one half to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: Tithes. Ownerless produce is exempt from them.

phrases.english: Come and hear: dried figs on the road,
and even beside a field of dried figs,
phrases.notes: That is a field where people spread figs out to dry, so you might think these figs came from there.

phrases.english: and likewise a fig tree leaning over the road,
and he found figs beneath it –
they are permitted, and taking them is not robbery,
and they are exempt from tithes.
With olives and carobs – it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new source brought to test the אביי and רבא dispute, after the proof from נמושות was pushed away in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: The dispute over יאוש שלא מדעת

steps.title: The first part of the משנה fits אביי
steps.stepSummary: The fig cases fit אביי. Dried figs are valuable, so the owner keeps checking them. Fig owners also know their figs fall, so they give up from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, the first part is no problem for אביי. Dried figs are valuable, so the owner keeps feeling for them and notices quickly. With the fig tree too, he surely knows that figs fall off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the fig cases do not disprove אביי. In each case the owner really does know about his loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking the figs seems to show that giving up without knowing counts. But אביי can say the owner did know. He checks his valuable dried figs often, and he expects a fig tree to drop fruit. So his giving up was a knowing one.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, this part is fine (the next part is the problem)
The first part of a משנה or ברייתא
Giving up on an item without knowing it was lost

phrases.english: Granted, the first part is not difficult for Abaye:
since they are valuable, he feels for them.
phrases.notes: Just like the money pouch in step 15, the owner keeps checking, so he notices right away when they are gone.

phrases.english: A fig tree too:
he surely knows that it drops its fruit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the first part of the משנה from step 20 fits אביי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the giving up in the case was a knowing one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Permitting the fallen figs seems to prove that giving up without knowing counts, against אביי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner knows about his loss, either because he checks often or because he expects the fruit to fall. So this is not a case of יאוש שלא מדעת.

steps.title: The last part of the משנה challenges רבא
steps.stepSummary: The rule that olives and carobs are forbidden seems hard for רבא. It suggests that giving up without knowing does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the last part is difficult for רבא, because it teaches: with olives and carobs, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבא and says the last line of the משנה seems to go against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner of fallen olives does not know yet that they fell, just like with the figs. According to רבא, his later giving up should already count, so the olives should be permitted. Since the משנה forbids them, it looks like giving up without knowing does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: But the last part is difficult for Rava,
for it teaches: "With olives and carobs, it is forbidden."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After showing the first part fits אביי, the גמרא shows the last part seems to go against רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that יאוש שלא מדעת counts as giving up
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fallen olives are a case where the owner does not know yet. If רבא were right, they would be permitted. The משנה forbids them.

steps.title: An olive is different because it shows whose it is
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו says an olive is different. It looks just like the olives on the tree, so everyone knows it belongs to the tree's owner, and the owner never gives up on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: an olive is different, since its look shows where it came from. Even though olives fall, everyone knows that what is in a person's place belongs to that person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו defends רבא by explaining that the olive case is not really about giving up without knowing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if olives fall, the owner does not give up on them. A fallen olive can be clearly matched to his tree, so he expects people to return it or leave it alone. With no giving up at all, the olives stay forbidden, even according to רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Its appearance proves where it came from

steps.confusionAlert: רבי אבהו is not saying that giving up without knowing doesn't count. He is saying that here the owner never gives up at all, so the debate between אביי and רבא doesn't even come up.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said: An olive is different,
since its appearance proves about it,
phrases.notes: A fallen olive looks just like the ones still on the tree, so you can tell which tree it came from.

phrases.english: and even though olives fall,
it is well known
that a person's place belongs to that person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבא from step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the case is different: there is no giving up at all
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Forbidding olives proves that giving up without knowing does not count.
steps.terutzMaskana: Olives are forbidden because the owner never gives up on them, since they are easy to identify. This has nothing to do with יאוש שלא מדעת.

steps.title: Then figs should be forbidden too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if that is the reason, then figs under a fig tree also show where they came from, so they should be forbidden too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even the first part should be forbidden too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבהו's answer by using it against the fig case in the first part of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fig lying under a fig tree also clearly shows which tree it came from. So by רבי אבהו's reasoning, the owner should not give up on it, and it should be forbidden. But the משנה permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your reason is right)

phrases.english: If so, even the first part too!
phrases.notes: He means the figs under the fig tree should also be forbidden, since you can tell which tree they came from.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אבהו's answer from step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's reason that the look of the fruit shows its owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Figs under a fig tree are just as easy to identify, yet the משנה permits them.

steps.title: A fallen fig gets spoiled
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that a fig gets spoiled when it falls. The owner doesn't want it anymore, so he gives up on it even though it can be identified.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: a fig becomes disgusting when it falls.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains why figs are different from olives, which saves רבי אבהו's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being able to identify the fruit only matters if the owner still wants it. A fallen fig gets bruised and spoiled, so the owner gives it up right away. An olive doesn't spoil from falling, so the owner keeps his claim to it.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה fits both sides. For אביי, the fig owners know about their loss. For רבא, olives are forbidden only because the owner never gives up on fruit that can be identified. Figs are permitted because a fallen fig is spoiled, so the owner doesn't want it anyway.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: תְּאֵנָה עִם נְפִילָתָהּ נִמְאֶסֶת.
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: A fig becomes disgusting with its fall.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: תְּאֵנָה עִם נְפִילָתָהּ נִמְאֶסֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24 and keeps רבי אבהו's answer standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a real difference between the cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Figs and olives can both be identified, so they should have the same rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: A fallen fig is spoiled, so its owner gives it up. An olive is not spoiled, so its owner keeps his claim.

steps.title: Opening a new proof: a thief or robber who passes an item to someone else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts quoting a ברייתא about a גנב or גזלן who took an item from one person and gave it to another. This sets up a new test for the argument over יאוש שלא מדעת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a thief who took something from one person and gave it to another, and also a robber who took something from one person and gave it to another...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new proof by quoting the first part of a ברייתא. The ruling has not been said yet. It comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just finished defending רבא's view. Now the גמרא brings a fresh source to test יאוש שלא מדעת again. The case is an item that ended up with a new person through a גנב or a גזלן. The question will be whether the new person may keep it, and what that tells us about the owner giving up.

keyTerms.meaning: A thief who steals in secret
A robber who takes openly, by force
Giving up hope on an item without knowing it was lost or taken. This is the topic the proof is testing.
And likewise. It adds another case with the same ruling.

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is not finished here. Don't look for the ruling or the proof yet. The ברייתא keeps going in the next lines.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A thief who took from this one and gave to that one,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן גַּזְלָן שֶׁנָּטַל מִזֶּה וְנָתַן לָזֶה,
phrases.english: and likewise a robber who took from this one and gave to that one,

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הַגַּנָּב שֶׁנָּטַל מִזֶּה וְנָתַן לָזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The olive and fig challenges to רבא are now answered, so the גמרא brings a new ברייתא to test יאוש שלא מדעת.
steps.raayaObject: The argument between אביי and רבא about whether יאוש שלא מדעת counts
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a גנב or גזלן who took an item from one person and gave it to another (the ruling comes next)
